ghost.sample: Zog was a small dragon. He lived behind the moon. Zog ate clouds every day. He liked the soft ones best. One day, Zog saw one tiny cloud. It was high and white. Zog wanted it very much. But the cloud moved away. Zog felt sad. Then he saw his friend Ben. Ben was on a bright moon hill. Ben waved and smiled. "I can help," said Ben. Ben held a stick up high. Zog flew near the cloud. He ate it with one happy bite. The cloud was yummy and cool. Ben clapped his hands. Zog smiled too. Then Zog went back behind the moon. He felt warm and happy. He had his cloud and his friend.

Zog was a small dragon. He lived behind the moon. He ate clouds every day, and nothing else. One day, he saw a cloud in a game of sky hide. The cloud hid behind the moon. Zog smiled. "I see you," he said. He flew around the moon and found it. Then the cloud hid again. Zog looked up, down, and around. At last, he found it near a bright star. He ate it and felt very happy. A little friend named Ben waved from far away. Ben said, "Good job, Zog!" Zog waved back. He felt proud and warm. Then he saw two more clouds and ate them too. Zog went home behind the moon. He looked at the star and smiled. The night was calm and sweet.

Sisi was a little cloud. Sisi lived in the sky. Sisi liked to sing songs. One day, Sisi saw a small bird under. The bird looked sad. It had lost a red toy in the grass. Sisi thought hard. Then Sisi sang a soft song. The song was happy and warm. The bird looked up. It smiled a little. Sisi went down close to the grass. The bird found its toy by a tree. "Thank you," said the bird. "You sang and helped me." Sisi smiled too. Then Sisi went back up. It was still in the sky. Sisi liked to sing songs again. The bird sang too. They made a nice song together. The sky felt very bright.

Sisi was a little cloud. Sisi lived in the sky. Sisi liked to sing songs.  
One day, Sisi flew by a big bird. The bird looked sad. He said, "I lost my toy." Sisi felt kind and wanted to help. Sisi sang a soft song and looked down. Soon, Sisi saw the toy on a tree. The toy was small and blue. Sisi called, "Bird, look up!" The bird saw it and smiled.  
The bird went to the tree and got his toy. "Thank you," he said. Sisi sang again, and the bird laughed. They played up in the sky for a little while. Then the bird flew home. Sisi felt very happy. Sisi sang a song all by the sun. The sky was warm and bright, and Sisi smiled too.

Pip was a tiny robot. Pip loved red apples. Pip slept in a teapot.  
One day, Pip went to the park with Tom. Tom had a big ball. Pip wanted to play too.  
But the ball rolled away. It went under a bench. Tom looked sad. Pip looked too.  
Pip said, "I can help." Pip rolled under the bench. Pip was small, so it fit.  
Pip pushed the ball out with its little hand. Tom smiled big. "Thank you, Pip!" he said.  
Then Pip saw a red apple on the grass. Pip loved red apples.  
Tom gave the apple to Pip. Pip was very happy.  
When the sun went down, Pip went home. Pip got into its teapot and slept.  
Pip dreamed of the park, the ball, and the red apple.

Pip was a tiny robot. Pip loved red apples, and Pip slept in a teapot every night. One day Pip and Ben went to the beach. The sand was soft, and the sky was blue. Pip saw a red apple in a picnic box. Pip said, "Can I have that?" Ben said, "Yes, you can." Pip took the red apple and smiled. Then a wave came close to the box. Ben felt worried. Pip was a tiny robot, so Pip could help. Pip moved the box back from the water. Ben said, "Good job, Pip!" They sat on a blanket and ate the apple. A crab walked by. Pip laughed. When the sun went down, Pip and Ben went home. Pip got into the teapot and slept. Pip felt happy and calm.

guide.answer:
To get stories for your character, you'll need to train your model. Since you're in single character mode with Zog, you can create prompts that include Zog's facts and let the model generate stories from there. Start with simple ideas, then build on them as you explore the training process.

guide.question: Why do some stories get turned away?
guide.answer: Stories can get turned away because they might not fit the patterns the model has learned or they don't align with the training examples it has seen. It's like a puzzle where the pieces need to match up. If a story is too different or doesn't make sense, it might not get accepted. DO: SHOW storybook.

guide.question: Why switch parts off instead of just looking at the attention?
guide.answer: Switching parts off helps us to measure causal contribution directly, while attention alone shows correlation. This way, we can determine if a specific part actually affects the prediction, rather than just being associated with it. Understanding both gives us a clearer picture of how the model works. guide.question: Why switch parts off instead of just looking at the attention?
guide.answer: Looking at attention can point to parts that seem connected, but it only shows a correlation, not a cause. Switching parts off tests whether those parts actually change the next word, though even that still does not prove one single place stores the fact.
